title: What Miles Davis Taught Herbie Hancock: In Music, as in Life, There Are No Mistakes, Just Chances to Improvise
description:
in Life, Music |   	July 28th, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			

	

One of my favorite Bri­an Eno quotes, or rather one that became an Oblique Strat­e­gy
body:
in Life, Music |   	July 28th, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			

	

One of my favorite Bri­an Eno quotes, or rather one that became an Oblique Strat­e­gy, is “Hon­or Your Mis­take as a Hid­den Inten­tion.” (Or to be pedan­tic, the orig­i­nal ver­sion was “Hon­or Thy Error…”).
As a teenag­er grow­ing up and try­ing to make art (at that time music and comics) there was no advice more free­ing. It was the oppo­site of what I thought I knew: mis­takes were shame­ful, the sign of an ama­teur or of the lack of prac­tice. But the more art I made, the more I ref­er­enced Eno’s idea, and the more I read and lis­tened, the more I real­ized it wasn’t just Eno.
The Bea­t­les left in an alarm clock meant for the musi­cians on “A Day in the Life” and the sound of emp­ty booze bot­tles vibrat­ing on a speak­er was left in at the end of “Long Long Long” (along with tons more). The Beast­ie Boys left in a jump­ing nee­dle intend­ed for a smooth scratch on “The Sounds of Sci­ence.” Radio­head left in Jon­ny Greenwood’s warm-up chord that became essen­tial to “Creep.” (There’s a whole Red­dit thread devot­ed to these mis­takes if you choose to go down the rab­bit hole.)
But those exam­ples relate to the record­ing process of rock music. What about jazz? Sure­ly there are “wrong” notes when it comes to play­ing, espe­cial­ly if you’re not the soloist.
In this very short video based around an inter­view with pianist Her­bie Han­cock, the mas­ter impro­vis­er Miles Davis hon­ored Hancock’s mis­take as a hid­den inten­tion by play­ing along with it. It’s both a sur­pris­ing look into the arcane world of jazz impro­vi­sa­tion and a reveal­ing anec­dote of Davis, usu­al­ly known as a dif­fi­cult col­lab­o­ra­tor.
“It taught me a very big les­son not only about music,” says Han­cock, “but about life.”
Note: An ear­li­er ver­sion of this post appeared on our site in 2016.
Relat­ed Con­tent:

 Ted Mills is a free­lance writer on the arts.

title: How a 13th-Century Monk Created a Prayer Manuscript by Writing Over—and Accidentally Preserving—Archimedes’ Groundbreaking Mathematical Works
description:
in History, Math |   	July 29th, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			

	

In Jerusalem of the year 1229, there lived a Greek Ortho­dox monk named Johannes My
body:
in History, Math |   	July 29th, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			

	

In Jerusalem of the year 1229, there lived a Greek Ortho­dox monk named Johannes Myronas. Need­ing some parch­ment for a prayer book, he grabbed some already-used pages, erased their exist­ing con­tent, and over them wrote down “prayers for the dead, prayers for repen­tance, bless­ings for the loaves at East­er, and even a prayer for those who were unrea­son­ably exclud­ed,” says math-and-sci­ence YouTu­ber Ben Syversen in the video above. Myronas may have ful­filled his reli­gious duty with­out using too much valu­able parch­ment, but he could­n’t have known the even greater rel­e­vance his actions would turn out to have had in the realm of math­e­mat­ics. For the pages he’d scrubbed were a Greek com­pi­la­tion con­tain­ing the only known copy of cer­tain works by the ancient poly­math Archimedes.
As it turns out, Myronas com­mit­ted per­haps the most notable act of inad­ver­tent preser­va­tion in the his­to­ry of math­e­mat­ics. We get the word palimpsest from the medieval prac­tice of over­writ­ing a page after first eras­ing what had been on it before, though incom­plete­ly; hence the mean­ing of mul­ti­ple lay­ers that have remained leg­i­ble over time.
In the case of what we now know as the Archimedes Palimpsest, that leg­i­bil­i­ty was achieved only with the aid of late twen­ti­eth-cen­tu­ry and ear­ly twen­ty-first-cen­tu­ry tech­nol­o­gy, in addi­tion to the painstak­ing con­ser­va­tion effort required to keep this tenth-cen­tu­ry doc­u­ment in more or less one piece. (And all of that was only pos­si­ble thanks to the epic his­tor­i­cal jour­ney the Palimpsest took, which end­ed in 1998 when it sold for $2 mil­lion at Christie’s to a tech fig­ure we’re only assured is not Bill Gates.)


	

You can learn more about that project from the TED Talk just above by its direc­tor, the late William Noel of Bal­ti­more’s Wal­ters Art Muse­um. Thanks to his ded­i­ca­tion and that of his team, we now have writ­ings of Archimedes like the Stom­a­chion, which deals with a kind of chil­dren’s puz­zle that turns out to have con­sid­er­able sim­i­lar­i­ties with an ear­ly prob­lem in the field of com­bi­na­torics, and more impor­tant­ly, The Method of Mechan­i­cal The­o­rems, an expla­na­tion of cal­cu­lus-like pro­ce­dures for deter­min­ing area or vol­ume. None of this proves that Archimedes was the inven­tor of com­bi­na­torics or cal­cu­lus, exact­ly, but it does show us just how much fur­ther he’d man­aged to push Greek math­e­mat­ics than we’d pre­vi­ous­ly known. Besides, any work that can bring togeth­er his­to­ri­ans, clas­si­cists, math­e­mati­cians, con­ser­va­tors, physi­cists, and com­put­er sci­en­tists more than two mil­len­nia after its com­po­si­tion sure­ly mer­its a place in the canon.
Relat­ed con­tent:

title: Hear What Homer’s Odyssey Sounded Like When Sung in the Original Ancient Greek
description:
in History, Literature, Music |   	July 29th, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			
Image via Wiki­me­dia Com­mons
It’s been a human­ist tru­ism for some time
body:
in History, Literature, Music |   	July 29th, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			
Image via Wiki­me­dia Com­mons
It’s been a human­ist tru­ism for some time to say that Shake­speare speaks to every age, tran­scend­ing his time and place through the sheer force of his uni­ver­sal genius. But any hon­est stu­dent first encoun­ter­ing the plays will tell you dif­fer­ent­ly, as will many a sea­soned schol­ar who works hard to place the writer and his work in his­tor­i­cal con­text. Even one­time direc­tor of London’s Nation­al The­atre, Nicholas Hyt­ner, once said, “I’ll admit that I hard­ly ever go to a per­for­mance of one of Shakespeare’s plays with­out expe­ri­enc­ing blind pan­ic dur­ing the first five min­utes. I sit there think­ing… I have no idea what these peo­ple are talk­ing about.”
Of course, none of that means we can’t learn to appre­ci­ate Shake­speare, and we do not need a grad­u­ate-lev­el edu­ca­tion to do so. But much of his archa­ic lan­guage and obscure ref­er­ences will always sound for­eign to mod­ern ears. How much more so, then, the lan­guage of the ancient Greeks, whether in trans­la­tion or not? Although we’ve also been taught to think of the Home­r­ic epics as con­tain­ers of uni­ver­sal truth and beau­ty, the world of Homer was, in many ways, an alien one—and the lit­er­a­ture of ancient Greece was far clos­er to song than even Shakespeare’s musi­cal speech­es.
In fact, “before writ­ing was gen­er­al­ly known among the Greeks,” the Uni­ver­si­ty of Cincin­nati notes, “poets recit­ed and sang sto­ries for audi­ences at the courts of city lead­ers and at fes­ti­vals. A poet could actu­al­ly impro­vise a tale in the six-beat rhythm of Greek verse if he knew the plot of his sto­ry.” We do not know whether Homer was one enter­pris­ing scribe or “a group of poets whose works on the theme of Troy were col­lect­ed” under one name. But in either case, that poet or poets heard the tales of Hec­tor and Achilles, Odysseus and Pene­lope, and all those med­dling gods sung before they wrote them down. Now, thanks to Georg Danek of the Uni­ver­si­ty of Vien­na and Ste­fan Hagel of the Aus­tri­an Acad­e­my of Sci­ences, we have some idea of what those songs may have sound­ed like.
“In the course of the last years,” write Danek and Hagel, “we have devel­oped a tech­nique of singing the Home­r­ic epics, which is appro­pri­ate for the pri­mar­i­ly oral tra­di­tion from which these poems emerge.” The two schol­ars cau­tion that their the­o­ret­i­cal recre­ations are “not to be under­stood as the exact recon­struc­tion of a giv­en melody, but as an approach to the tech­nique the Home­r­ic singers used to accom­mo­date melod­ic prin­ci­ples to the demands of the indi­vid­ual verse.” Accom­pa­nied by a four-stringed lyre-like instru­ment called a phorminx, “the Home­r­ic bard” would impro­vise the “melody at the same time as he impro­vised his text, which was unique in every per­for­mance.” In the audio above, you can hear Danek and Hagel’s melod­ic recre­ation of lines 267–366 of book 8 of the Odyssey, in which Demod­ocus sings about the love of Ares and Aphrodite.
At their site, the two schol­ars present an abstract of their Home­r­ic singing the­o­ry, with musi­co­log­i­cal and lin­guis­tic evi­dence for the recre­ation. Their tech­ni­cal cri­te­ria will con­fuse the non-spe­cial­ist, and none but ancient Greek speak­ers will under­stand the record­ing above. But it brings us a lit­tle clos­er to expe­ri­enc­ing Home­r’s epic poet­ry, “the foun­da­tion stones of Euro­pean Lit­er­a­ture,” as the ancient Greeks might have expe­ri­enced it.
If you would like to sup­port the mis­sion of Open Cul­ture, con­sid­er mak­ing a dona­tion to our site. It’s hard to rely 100% on ads, and your con­tri­bu­tions will help us con­tin­ue pro­vid­ing the best free cul­tur­al and edu­ca­tion­al mate­ri­als to learn­ers every­where. You can con­tribute through Pay­Pal, Patre­on, and Ven­mo (@openculture). Thanks!

title: Christopher Hitchens Explains Why Homer’s Odyssey Still Matters to Our World (2000)
description:
in Uncategorized |   	July 28th, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			

	

At the moment, the answer to the ques­tion of why we should read Home­r’s Odyssey s
body:
in Uncategorized |   	July 28th, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			

	

At the moment, the answer to the ques­tion of why we should read Home­r’s Odyssey seems rather straight­for­ward: so we can more intel­li­gent­ly voice our opin­ions on Christo­pher Nolan’s new block­buster film adap­ta­tion. A quar­ter-cen­tu­ry ago, the mat­ter was some­what less clear. Still, an occa­sion had pre­sent­ed itself in the form of a new Eng­lish trans­la­tion, by Uni­ver­si­ty of Kansas clas­sics pro­fes­sor Stan­ley Lom­bar­do. That book, and the work of Homer in gen­er­al, was the sub­ject of a live two-hour round­table dis­cus­sion aired on C‑SPAN’s Book TV in the fall of 2000, which, with the Odyssey back in the zeit­geist, appeared on YouTube just days ago.
Apart from Lom­bar­do him­self, the par­tic­i­pants include Joseph Bot­tum, then lit­er­ary edi­tor of the Week­ly Stan­dard; jour­nal­ist and mil­i­tary vet­er­an Debra J. Dick­er­son; and Christo­pher Hitchens, who clear­ly par­tic­i­pat­ed not just because he hap­pened to be liv­ing in Wash­ing­ton, D.C., but also out of a gen­uine appre­ci­a­tion for the Odyssey and an under­stand­ing of its rel­e­vance in the mod­ern world. Ear­ly on in the text, he explains, Homer intro­duces the con­cepts of hubris and neme­sis, which “we can­not do with­out in ordi­nary dis­course. There are cer­tain pun­ish­ments that appear to fall on peo­ple, for orig­i­nal arro­gance or con­ceit, that we can’t con­ceive of relat­ing grand sto­ries with­out.”
There’s the “caprice of the gods,” with which every reli­gion has had to deal, as well as the even more uni­ver­sal feel­ing of nos­tal­gia, “a very overused and sen­ti­men­tal­ized term now, which lit­er­al­ly means — and can only real­ly mean — the yearn­ing to go home.” Adduc­ing such re-inter­pre­ta­tions by writ­ers from Alexan­der Pope to James Joyce, Hitchens declares that we think of the Odyssey as “the orig­i­nal nar­ra­tive of the striv­ing of human­i­ty — and of the need, also, to beware of what you want, in case you ever do, as Cavafy says, final­ly get home to Itha­ca. It may turn out that it’s bet­ter to trav­el hope­ful­ly than to arrive.”
The mat­ter of virtue also aris­es in the con­ver­sa­tion, and specif­i­cal­ly whether the range of virtues of which Homer sang (up to and includ­ing luck) would be rec­og­nized in our Chris­t­ian or post-Chris­t­ian world. To the avowed­ly athe­ist Hitchens’ mind, of course, we should already have been post-reli­gious. Home­r’s deities are “anthro­po­mor­phic gods; they are invent­ed by us, as all gods are.” But what­ev­er your reli­gion or lack there­of, “if you don’t know some­thing about clas­si­cal Greece, then you won’t be able, with much prof­it, to read Shake­speare, or Mil­ton, or Shel­ley, or Keats, or even Chaucer. It would be like not know­ing what the bible sto­ry was and then won­der­ing how you puz­zle your way through Shake­speare as well. It’s part of the under­lay; it’s part of the com­mon her­itage.” The trans­la­tions and re-inter­pre­ta­tions have kept com­ing, but Homer him­self still patient­ly awaits each of us.

title: Nature or Culture? Europeans Can Vote on the New Banknote Design
description: What best represents European life? The eternal dichotomy of nature vs. culture structures the Central Bank’s quest for a new banknote design, and
body:
What best represents European life? The eternal dichotomy of nature vs. culture structures the Central Bank’s quest for a new banknote design, and now, the public can vote and offer feedback on ten proposals. 
A panel of jurors selected the designs, which follow one of two themes: European places and ideas or birds and rivers, the latter of which is meant to symbolize freedom and unity. While the basic elements are the same—all collections devoted to culture feature the same six figures, including Renaissance artist Leonardo da Vinci, composer Ludwig van Beethoven, scientist Marie Curie, opera singer Maria Callas, and authors Bertha von Suttner and Miguel de Cervantes, for example—individual approaches appear in the layout, aesthetic, and composition.
Voting is open through mid-September, when jurors will select one design that will go through an additional vetting process before the organization adopts it entirely. View all ten on the bank’s website.
Rudy Guedj and François Girard-Meunier

title: August 2026 Opportunities: Open Calls, Residencies, and Grants for Artists
description: Every month, we share opportunities for artists and designers, including open calls, grants, fellowships, and residencies. Make sure you never mis
body:
Every month, we share opportunities for artists and designers, including open calls, grants, fellowships, and residencies. Make sure you never miss out by joining our monthly Opportunities Newsletter.
Nuditas 2026: 5th Annual Juried Exhibition, Publication, Promotion, and SalesFeaturedReady to reveal the naked truth of the human body? From personal identity and body positivity to spirituality, mythology, emotion, and vulnerability, Nuditas 2026 celebrates the human form in all its expressions. Submit your strongest figurative or abstract works for the opportunity to exhibit internationally, be featured on Artsy, published in the official catalogue, and promoted worldwide.Learn more and submit: www.exhibizone.com/nuditasDeadline: 11:59 p.m. PST on August 13, 2026.
Arch Enemy Arts Call for ArtistsFeaturedArch Enemy Arts is seeking submissions for an annual group exhibition in January 2027. This spotlight exhibition of new and emerging talent has no themes or direction in subject matter, although the gallery focuses on representational, dark surrealism, magical realism, post-graffiti, pop-surrealism, narrative, illustrative, and figurative work across a range of artistic mediums. The exhibition is open to artists worldwide, who are invited to submit up to three works for consideration.Deadline: 11:59 p.m. EST on November 13, 2026.
Open Calls
The British Art Prize (International)The British Art Prize, run by Artists & Illustrators magazine, is one of the U.K.’s most exciting annual art competitions showcasing the talent and diversity of contemporary artists from around the world. Each year, a panel of leading curators, gallerists, and art professionals selects a shortlist of outstanding works. These finalists are exhibited at London’s Oxo Gallery. Winners are awarded prizes worth more than £10,000, including cash awards, art materials, a solo exhibition at Panter & Hall’s Cecil Court Gallery, and editorial features in Artists & Illustrators.Deadline: 5 p.m. BST on August 7, 2026.
Clotilda Memorial Alabama Historical Commission (International)The Alabama Historical Commission is seeking proposals to honor the last known African captives trafficked to the United States through the transatlantic slave trade: the Clotilda survivors. The memorial will convey dimensions of the survivors’ lives and legacies—celebrating their resilient and determined spirits amidst violent dislocation, enslavement, and discrimination. Projects will be developed through a collaborative process that will engage the community founded by the Clotilda survivors and other formerly enslaved people: historic Africatown and the expansive diaspora. The total budget is $2,000,000.Deadline: 11:59 p.m. CDT on August 9, 2026.
Publish Your Art in Artistonish Magazine and Sell on Artsy(International)Submit works of art for the 73rd issue of Artistonish Contemporary Art Magazine, featuring juried contemporary works online and on premium glossy print pages. Each selected artwork receives a full-page image, dedicated QR code, Artsy feature for sales visibility, certificate of achievement, exclusive artwork badges, global promotion, and lasting online presence within the international art community. There is no fee to apply; selected artists pay a selection fee of $45.Deadline: 11:59 p.m. PDT on August 11, 2026.
The Wild Canvas Sketch Challenge to Win a Puerto Rico Art Retreat(International)The Wild Canvas is organizing its inaugural art retreat in Ceiba, Puerto Rico, which invites up to 12 artists for a week-long program in January 2027. A sketching contest around the theme of “Island Time” provides a chance to win a fully funded spot, plus additional scholarships.Deadline: August 25, 2026.
AMPLIFY Mural Open Call(U.S.)The Spruill Gallery in Dunwoody, Georgia, is accepting nationwide submissions for its annual AMPLIFY mural competition. The winning artist will receive a $10,000 prize, and their mural will adorn the side of the historic Spruill Smoke House for the coming year.Deadline: 11:59 p.m. EDT on August 28, 2026.
ARTLittle 1st International Metaverse Art Expo (International)The 1st International Metaverse Art Expo, presented by ARTLittle, is a 3D multiuser online exhibition where visitors from around the world walk through the galleries with avatars, discover artworks, and buy directly. ARTLittle is an independent art project built in Malaysia and is open to artists and galleries worldwide. Three hundred artists will be selected for exhibition in the virtual expo and have works offered for sale.Deadline: 11:59 p.m. MYT on August 31, 2026.
Hunt Museum Open Submission Exhibition (International)The Hunt Open Submission Exhibition is an initiative celebrating contemporary Irish and international art at the Hunt Museum in Limerick. There is a €15 entry fee for the first image, plus an additional €15 per artwork for up to three submissions.Deadline: September 7, 2026.
Hiding in Plain Site: International Public Art Short Film Festival (International)HPS invites filmmakers, artists, and creative practitioners to submit short works between two and 20 minutes for consideration in this screening program, which will premiere on October 25 in Minneapolis. HPS seeks to bring together film, video art, experimental media, XR (extended reality), and other works that expand how public art is experienced and represented. Deadline: September 10, 2026.
Apply to Teach at Mendocino Art Center (U.S.)The Mendocino Art Center (MAC), located in the coastal Northern California community of Mendocino, offers workshops taught by both visiting and local artists in a wide variety of mediums and topics. Some instructors choose to be compensated, and some choose to teach pro bono to help MAC offer more affordable workshops.Deadline: Rolling.
Grants
Big Fields Fund Grants for Eastern Iowa Artists (Iowa)The Big Field Fund awards grants to artists and collectives to support publicly-engaged experimental, collaborative, and connective visual arts projects in eastern Iowa. Project grants award $8,000 to support the public realization of artist-led projects, while research and development grants offer $3,000 to support artists in the early stages of an ambitious project.Deadline: August 1, 2026.
SKOG Art Space Exhibitions Open Call (International)This open call welcomes artists from around the world at all career stages to apply for both solo and group exhibitions at SKOG in Oslo, Norway. The gallery welcomes proposals from both emerging and established artists working across all media and techniques.Deadline: August 16, 2026.
Midwest Culture Bearers Award (Midwest)The Midwest Culture Bearers Award honors and amplifies the work of 18 mid-career and established Midwestern cultural practitioners each year. Selected individuals will each receive a $5,000 unrestricted award. No cost share or match is required to receive these funds. Additionally, Arts Midwest offers awardees virtual professional development and networking opportunities, plus the opportunity to have a story written about their work.Deadline: August 18, 2026.
2027 Brightwork Fellowship & Grants (North Carolina)Anchorlight, based in Raleigh, offers one fellowship and two grants for 2027. The Professional Development Grant amounts to $2,000, and the Studio Project Grant awards $3,000. The fellowship is a year-long program geared toward an artist who is at a pivotal point in their career, providing a 500+ square-foot studio space at Anchorlight, an exhibition opportunity in its gallery, and an unrestricted financial award of $50,000. One artist will be selected for each, and each must have lived in North Carolina for at least 12 months as of applying. There is a $10 application fee for each opportunity.Deadline: August 28, 2026.
2026 Chrysalis Award for Emerging Ceramic Artists (U.S.)The Chrysalis Award was created by the James Renwick Alliance for Craft to support and inspire emerging craft artists in the United States. Eligible applicants are in the early stages of their professional artistic careers—regardless of age—and have completed their training within the past five years. This year’s award will recognize an emerging artist working in ceramics, who will receive a $5,000 unrestricted award, a one-year JRACraft membership, and the opportunity to present their work at a JRACraft event.Deadline: August 23, 2026.
Liu Shiming Artist Grants (U.S.)Designed to support the work of visual artists during the first decade of their careers, the Liu Shiming Artist Grants support the creation or completion of new projects that explore the interplay between traditional cultural or historical influences and contemporary artistic practice. Up to five artists will be selected to receive a $5,000 grant.Deadline: August 31, 2026.
Dezi Art Prize (International)This global juried art grant is geared toward emerging and early-career visual artists. Two winners each receive a $1,000 unrestricted grant, plus a featured profile. Ten finalists are named and featured. Open worldwide, all visual media is welcome, with entries scored on merit by an independent jury. There is a $30 application fee.Deadline: September 10, 2026.
Printed Matter Publisher Work Grant (International)Now in its third year, Printed Matter’s Publisher Work Grant program offers funding to independent presses with a history of artists’ book publishing, acknowledging awardees’ accomplishments in past work and providing the capacity-building funds to enable future book projects and publisher sustainability. In 2026, three unrestricted grants of $10,000 will be awarded to three independent artists’ book publishers. Printed Matter will also extend a featured exhibitor presence at a forthcoming Printed Matter NY or LA Art Book Fair to selected presses.Deadline: October 4, 2026.
ARRIVAL Gallery Micro Grant (International)The ARRIVAL Grant is designed to keep support simple and accessible. Artists submit one original artwork to the current round, and once the round reaches 1,000 valid submissions, one eligible artist receives a £100 grant and a new round begins.Deadline: Rolling.
The Adolf and Esther Gottlieb Emergency Grant (International)This program provides one-time financial assistance to qualified painters, printmakers, and sculptors whose needs resulted from an unforeseen catastrophic incident and who lack the resources to meet that situation. Awardees typically receive $5,000 and up to $15,000.Deadline: Rolling.
Pollock-Krasner Foundation Grant (International)The foundation welcomes applications from painters, sculptors, and artists working on paper, including printmakers. Grants are intended for one year and range up to $50,000. The artist’s circumstances determine the size of the grant, and professional exhibition history will be considered.Deadline: Rolling.
Residencies, Fellowships, & More
BigCi Environmental Awards 2026 (International)Australian and international artists working in visual art, installation, multimedia, performance, literature, music, photography, filmmaking, and curating are invited to submit entries for the BigCi Environmental Awards 2026. Two winning artists will each receive a free four-week residency at BigCi, where they will have the opportunity to explore the UNESCO World Heritage-listed Wollemi, Blue Mountains, and Gardens of Stone National Parks in Australia. The winners also receive an AUD$5,000 award. There is an AUD$40 application fee.Deadline: August 2, 2026.
TaDA Residency 2027 (International)Each year, six jury-selected candidates have the opportunity to work with textile companies in Eastern Switzerland, use a local studio in Arbon, and extend their individual networks over a period of three months. At the TaDA Spinnerei event, also attended by international speakers, artists can present their projects to an interested public and discuss with experts.Deadline: August 12, 2026.
Surface Design Association Artist-in-Residence Program (International)The residency program facilitated by the Surface Design Association (SDA) is designed to build skills, leverage relationships, and offer support to early, mid-career, and established fiber artists as they undertake studio projects that inspire artistic growth. The residency is virtual, and the selected participant is provided with a $2,000 studio stipend to support projects during their time. There is no application fee, but applicants must be members of SDA.Deadline: August 14, 2026.
Center for Performance Research AiR (New York City)CPR’s residency supports artists working in contemporary dance, performance, and time-based art. The organization values experimental approaches to content, form, and aesthetics and encourages risk-taking, interdisciplinarity, and the unexpected. The residency runs for one year (January to December 2027) and includes a $2,000 stipend, 20 free hours of rehearsal space, and more.Deadline: 5 p.m. EDT on August 24, 2026.
bEam arts Residency (International)bEam arts is an independent, artist-led residency program located in Thessaloniki, Greece, which welcomes visual artists and writers. The program supports a vibrant studio practice for up to four visual artists and two writers to stay for one or two months. During the residency, bEam arts hosts monthly activities and provides artists with opportunities to connect, engage with one another, and expand their professional networks. Each cycle ends with a group exhibition. The cost is €1,850 per month, including accommodation.Deadline: August 24, 2026.
AVISTAVULCÃO Residency (Europe)Part of the Culture Moves Europe initiative, this open call is for applications for a one-month artist-in-residence program focused on research and creation, to take place in March 2027, intended for an artist or artistic duo. Located on the Azares island of Faial, near the Capelinhos Volcano, the residency offers an immersion in a territory shaped by the power of geology, its insular nature, and the constant interplay between nature and human presence. Deadline: August 31, 2026.
Helpmann Fellowships (South Australia)Three Helpmann Fellowships of up to AUD $7,500 are available to support ambitious, self-directed projects that advance the artistic and professional development of recent graduates (within five years) of eligible performing and visual arts programs at South Australia’s two universities. Funding can support larger-scale creative projects, tailored professional development, or a combination of both.Deadline: 11:59 p.m. ACST on August 31, 2026.
2027 National Gallery of Iceland Residency(International)The National Gallery of Iceland is seeking applications to its CUSP program, a European cooperation project funded through Creative Europe’s Culture grant. Artists working in complex media or emerging technologies are invited to apply. The residency will be up to four weeks long, and accommodation, workspace, and stipends are provided.Deadline: 11:59 p.m. GMT on September 2, 2026.
ON::View Artist Residency Program(International)Located in the heart of Savannah’s Starland District at ARTS Southeast, the fully-funded ON::View Artist Residency provides a free, high-visibility studio space, lodging, and a $500 stipend for an artist or curator to complete a new project, continue an in-progress endeavor, or to conduct research. There is a $50 application fee.Deadline: 11:59 p.m. ET on September 7, 2026.
MacDowell Fellowships for Spring/Summer 2027(International)Located in Peterborough, New Hampshire, MacDowell encourages applications from artists of all backgrounds and all countries in the following disciplines: architecture, film/video, interdisciplinary arts, literature, music composition, theatre, and visual arts. A Fellowship consists of exclusive use of a private studio, accommodations, and three prepared meals a day for two to eight weeks.Deadline: September 10, 2026.
2027-28 QM-Jerome Foundation Fellowship for Emerging Artists(New York City)The Queens Museum (QM) launches its eighth iteration of the QM-Jerome Foundation Fellowship for Emerging Artists in New York City. Two visual artists will receive $20,000 each and professional development consultations from QM staff members working toward an artist’s project. Each fellow will also receive mentorship from a New York-based established artist. The fellowships will culminate in solo project exhibitions at the Queens Museum in 2028. The duration of each fellowship is one year, culminating with the opening of the fellow’s exhibition.Deadline: 11:59 p.m. EDT on September 28, 2026.
Quarantine (International)Dubbed “purgatory for artists,” Quarantine is a week-long intensive art program on an 18th-century quarantine island off the coast of Menorca, Spain. The program is open to beginners and professionals alike and offers three 45-minute private mentorships throughout the week, with activities lasting 12+ hours per day. Phones are banned.Deadline: Rolling.
Residencia Corazón (International)Residencia Corazón is an independent, artist-run residency in LaPlata, Argentina—a home for artists since 2006. The program welcomes visualartists, writers, curators, and creative researchers from around theworld for one- to three-month residencies. Each stay is fully personalized, and fees range from $800 to $1,500 per month.Deadline: Rolling.

title: Innovation Meets Heritage in West African Contemporary Artists' Masquerade Ensembles

body:
Across West Africa, Indigenous communities mark holidays, rites, and sacred events with a remarkable variety of ceremonies ranging from dances to processions. These masquerade traditions incorporate meticulously carved masks and full-body costumes that often facilitate links between humans and the spiritual world. There’s evidence of masked customs dating back millennia, and today, artists continue the tradition of hand-hewn masks and ensembles in vivid colors and a wide array of materials—sometimes with a twist.
The exhibition New African Masquerades: Artistic Innovations and Collaborations, which opens at the Museum of Fine Arts St. Petersburg next month, celebrates contemporary creations by four artists: Chief Ekpenyong Bassey Nsa (Nigeria), David Sanou (Burkina Faso), Sheku “Goldenfinger” Fofanah (Sierra Leone), and Hervé Youmbi (Cameroon). Along with displays of some of their masks and full ensembles, visitors will be able to explore documentary photographs and videos of ceremonies and parades in addition to immersive multimedia experiences.
Headpiece by André Sanou and body by anonymous artist, “Kimi” masquerade ensemble in honor of André Sanou’s ‘Qui Dit Miuex?’ (2022). Collection of Fitchburg Art Museum, photo courtesy of the New Orleans Museum of Art
“Across many West African cultures, masquerade a broad range of artistic, social, spiritual, and civic traditions,” the museum says. “Encompassing sculpture, textiles, performance, music, movement, and community participation, these performance traditions continuously adapt to contemporary life.” Sanou’s geometric masks are bold and brightly painted, often paired with costumes made from colorfully dyed fiber. And one can even spot pop culture references in Youmbi’s “Tso Scream Mask,” for example, which coats the iconic visage from the Scream movie franchise with thousands of beads.
New African Masquerades is conceived as a dynamic exploration of the masquerade tradition’s collaborative and community-based practices, inviting viewers to a kind of reverie where time-honored heritage meets constant innovation. The show is organized by the New Orleans Museum of Art in partnership with the Museé des Civilisations noires in Dakar, Senegal. The exhibition opens on August 15 and continues through January 3, 2027, in St. Pete, Florida. Follow updates on the museum’s Instagram.
Hervé Youmbi (Cameroon), “Tso Scream Mask” from the ‘Visage de masques (IX) series’ (2015-2023), wood, pigment, fiber, beads, textile, glue, velvet fabric, cotton fabric, silk embroidery, and horse hair. Collection of the New Orleans Museum of Art
Hervé Youmbi, “Tso Scream Mask” and “Tso Scream Leopard Mask” at the Nka’a Kossié society succession ceremony at Fondanti Chieftancy (December 3, 2022). Photo by Hervé Youmbi, courtesy of the artist and Axis Gallery, New York and New Jersey
Sheku “Goldenfinger” Fofanah (Sierra Leone), “Fairy Masquerade Ensemble” (2022), fabric, sequins, wood, paint, and glue, life-size. Commission for the Fitchburg Art Museum, photo courtesy of the New Orleans Museum of Art
Hervé Youmbi, “Bamiléké-Kwele Ku’ngang Gorilla Mask” and “Single-faced Rhino Mask” during a ceremony in Fondanti village (2019). Photo by Hervé Youmbi, courtesy of the artist and Axis Gallery, New York and New Jersey
Headpieces by David Sanou, studio of André Sanou, “Kimi” masks during a performance of greetings with the lead griot Tchiedo playing his drum behind them (May 3, 2022),  Bindougosso district, Bobo-Dioulasso, Burkina Faso. Photo by Lisa Homann
Chief Ekpenyong Bassey Nsa (Nigeria), “Afia Awan Masquerade Ensemble” (2022), polyester fabric, raffia, and leather, life-size. Collection of the New Orleans Museum of Art
Sheky “Goldenfinger” Fofanah parading with his Mami Wata devil during the Massaboni Ordehlay procession (December 26, 2022), Lunsar, Sierra Leone. Photo by Amanda M. Maples
